title: Pakistan has locked down Imran Khan's stronghold - but it could backfire
content: Schools closed. The internet partially shut. Roads blocked by shipping containers. And the army arriving in town. Imran Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is under a state of emergency, his party's provincial government suspended. It's another dramatic escalation in the standoff between the former prime minister's supporters and Pakistan's state - and one that some fear could lead to more instability, not less. According to the federal government this step, allowed by the constitution, was needed to provide protection for the province's population from the threat of terror. "The PTI KPK government was hand in glove with the terrorists," Attah Tarrar, federal information minister, told journalists on Sunday. He did not elaborate or provide evidence, but promised to do so soon. Two days later there had still been no update from him - but schools had reopened in Peshawar and most parts of the province, and internet services had been restored. While police would not confirm any detentions, there is clearly a crackdown under way to prevent protests. Most PTI leaders in the province have gone into hiding. On Tuesday dozens of PTI supporters took to the streets in Bara, Khyber district, hometown of provincial Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. There were reports of tear gas shelling in the area. To many observers, the timing of Sunday's announcement of emergency rule is not coincidental. For the last week, thousands of Imran Khan's supporters have marched through Khyber Pakhtunkhwa , where the PTI have been in power for 13 years, demanding Khan's release. "The charitable response would be to say that it sounded disingenuous," says Farzana Sheikh, associate fellow at Chatham House. "I do not see the link with terrorism," says Arifa Noor, journalist and commentator. "I'm not even sure if it was the long march itself [that led to this]. Perhaps it was the last straw or perhaps it's just a case of saying, we don't want to deal with the government being in the hands of an opposition party." The protests were led by Chief Minister Afridi, whose whereabouts are still a mystery. His party says he has been arrested; the government says that he is in protective custody. Before the march had begun, there had been a crackdown. Three of Khan's sisters were arrested in September , accused among other things of mobilising supporters, and have been detained ever since. Khan has barely been seen by his family or lawyers in the last year; two of his sisters saw him in August, one in prison, another as he was checked over at a hospital visit after concerns were raised by the Supreme Court about his health, before he was returned behind bars again where he has been held for more than three years. The PTI leader, who is widely believed to have lost power because of a rift with Pakistan's powerful military, has been imprisoned since August 2023. He is convicted in several corruption cases which he says are politically motivated. With the party already weakened, why this reaction from the authorities? "The PTI rank and file has been becoming increasingly restless in recent months amid growing concerns about Imran Khan's health," says Michael Kugelman, senior South Asia fellow at the Atlantic Council. "There is a sense that perhaps now is the time to send a very strong message to the party and make it more difficult for them to be able to put pressure on the government." The government has previously argued that Khan was going against jail rules by using his meetings to discuss politics. Tarar has said of the state of emergency: "There was no political agenda. They could have gone on with their march," and pointed to the talks the two sides had in the run-up to the decision as an indicator that they did try discussion. But others see this as just another attempt to restrict Khan and his party. "The government has less and less space for disagreements or dissent and they do not want to negotiate their way out of any kind of conflict," Noor says. Zahid Hussain, Islamabad-based author and defence analyst, is clear about who is behind the decision. "The balance of power is completely shifted to the military establishment," he says. Sheikh thinks that Pakistan's military is feeling confident because it believes it has a good relationship with the White House, its international credentials burnished by their role in the US-Iran peace talks. "The mode is very much, this is the moment, let's seize it," she says. "There is a sense that, we have all the cards in our hands. We can ride this out internationally." But Pakistan has plenty to contend with. Militancy is rising. The country was ranked number one in the Global Terrorism Index 2026 as the country which had been affected most. The country is at loggerheads with two neighbours; it has repeatedly hit Afghanistan with air strikes accusing the Afghan Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, a claim it denies. It would take little to reignite its long-running simmering conflict with India. Meanwhile, it has promised to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against attacks as the conflict against the Houthis has become increasingly dangerous. Short of solving one problem, some have warned this state of emergency could lead to more challenges. It risks increasing political instability, with Islamabad taking responsibility for a province without a buffer - the provincial government - they can blame. "I would argue that this could actually backfire," Kugelman says. "You're playing with fire because if this move ends up adding to the anger and the discontent among so many there, then you have a very big problem on your hands." "It is reckless, given the challenges, multiple challenges the country is facing," Hussain says. He fears that more of these powers could be used across Pakistan. Attempts to combat militancy with more active army operations could come with its own perils too, Sheikh argues. "If they're going to launch these operations, they're going to have to be prepared to accept casualties of members of the armed forces," she says. If those are significant, it could lead to questions inside the military institution, she adds. Pakistan, with its history of military coups, has examples in its past where removing elected governments, whether provincial or national, can turn sour. "It's not that senior people in the PML-N [the party in federal government] don't realise that some of these things can come back and haunt them in the future," Noor says. "Similarly I think to some extent the PTI realises that they will not be able to hold a protest and get Imran Khan out. I think that's the most unfortunate part of this mess that we're in, that we are going into it with our eyes wide open. "Everybody realises that this is a train crash but somehow you can't stop it." Thousands have taken to the streets after talks between authorities and Khan's party ended in deadlock. Aleema Khanum is accused of mobilising her brother’s supporters ahead of country-wide protests. The former skippers say it is "basic decency" for Pakistan to comply with a court-ordered medical assessment. It comes as the court had earlier this week ordered that he had to be taken for a hospital examination. Imran Khan has been imprisoned since 2023 on corruption charges which he says were politically motivated. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children'
content: In China's cities, despite the huge crowds, or maybe because of them, residents can feel very isolated. Now, a new industry being dubbed the "loneliness economy" has emerged, with people hiring themselves out as companions to help the elderly. The BBC's China correspondent Stephen McDonell visits a company that does just that, to see how their business works. Read more about the paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely. Reports say a gas leak at a fried chicken shop may be behind the blast, which killed two and injured 26. With Super Tuesday underway in the US, the BBC asks China's elite who they want to win this year's election. At least nine people were injured in the incident, which Chinese state media said involved over 100 cars. A trained economist, Li was once tipped to be the country's future leader. The highest level of storm alert is in effect in Hong Kong, with people being warned to stay indoors. China police issue warnings after a child is seen playing hide and seek on the side of a apartment building. Giant panda at Wolong Shenshuping, China, looks very relaxed whilst they have the hiccups Video from China’s Sichuan province shows the animal looking relaxed, but unimpressed. The rescue was shown on Chinese state TV as devastating floods hit Hebei province. Parts of China have been hit by an onslaught of extreme weather, causing widespread flooding. This video has been removed for rights reasons. The blast was caused by a leaking liquefied petroleum gas tank, state media reports. Harrowing video shows people trying to escape a fire in Beijing that killed 29 people. On land, by sea and in the air - pictures released by China's state broadcaster show military drills around Taiwan. The BBC's Celia Hatton breaks down Xi Jinping's caffeine habits, and why they might be a subtle power play. As China deals with a new Covid wave, Ros Atkins looks at why it’s hard to assess its scale. Jimmy and Tommy Lindesay are covering the equivalent of a marathon every day for six months. People in Beijing see a cautious return to life after China lifts its most severe Covid restrictions. There were widespread protests after 10 people died in a tower block fire in the city of Urumqi. Protests in Guangzhou continue a week of unrest in the country, aimed at the country's zero-Covid policy. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Pictured: Winning entries for Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026
content: An emotional scene of an elephant carrying a deceased calf has earned Italian photographer Federico Veronesi the title of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026. While tracking elephants in Namibia's Huab River Valley, Veronesi spotted an unusual trail of drag marks across the sand of a dry riverbed. Following the tracks, he came across a female elephant carrying a dead calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk. Initially, Veronesi assumed the elephant was the calf's mother. But after sharing his photographs with an elephant research project working in the area, he learned that this wasn't certain. Researchers recognised the elephant as a female who had lost a calf several years earlier and said she had previously picked up dead calves belonging to other females. For Veronesi, the encounter was deeply significant. "Of all the 20 years I've done photographing animals, this is the most heart-wrecking and fascinating and dramatic," he said, describing it as "revealing of the depth and complexity of the emotions, the feelings of the animals." He hopes the image will encourage people to look beyond animals' physical appearance and recognise them as individuals with their own relationships, memories and emotions. "It's a small window that opens just a crack into the complexity of their world," he said. The competition's annual exhibition opens at the Natural History Museum on Friday 16 October 2026. Keep scrolling to see more award-winning images. Category : Young Grand Title and 11 to 14 Years Photographer : Oscar Whitfield, Zimbabwe/UK Location : Zambezi National Park, Zimbabwe Only by lying in the dust and capturing the beetle at eye level could Whitfield show how much strength its task required. While on a family game drive in Zimbabwe, near his home in Victoria Falls, he spotted the dung beetle struggling to push a ball of dung uphill through the sand, with a trail of flies following closely behind. After experimenting with different angles and compositions, he captured a moment that reveals the extraordinary effort involved in this seemingly simple task. "I hope that when people look at the photograph, they can see too, and maybe appreciate how much can be happening in a small moment in the natural world," says Whitfield. Category : 10 Years and Under Photographer : Amelie Davis, UK Location : Surrey, England You do not need a camera or a plane ticket to take an award-winning photo. Davis captured this shot in the garden using her dad's smartphone. The image freezes in time a single wingbeat from a common carder bumblebee as it prepares to land on a flower. Category : Animals in their Environment Photographer : James Lewin, UK Location : Chyulu Hills National Park, Kenya Lewin captured this dreamy, black-and-white photo of a young bull elephant spraying zebras at a waterhole. He softened the usually harsh light by using a camera converted to infrared. Category : Animal Portraits Photographer : Aaron Sanders, UK Location : Porthkerris Beach, Cornwall Common octopuses are usually found in the warmer Mediterranean Sea. But with global warming pushing up springtime sea temperatures, sightings across south-west England have massively increased. Sanders described the moment he spotted a single eye peeking from behind the kelp: "We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity." Category : Birds Photographer : Isak Pretorius, South Africa Location : Mabamba Swamp, Uganda Fewer than 5,300 mature shoebill storks are estimated to remain in the wild. Yet Pretorius, while canoeing with a guide, was able to capture these two – likely a breeding pair collecting material for their nest. Despite their name, shoebill storks are actually more closely related to pelicans, herons and ibises. Category : 15-17 Years Photographer : Konrad Gräeter, Germany Location : Baden-Württemberg, Germany Spring sees male blackbirds search for high vantage points to sing and try to attract a mate. This photo was taken in a vineyard at dawn, when the birds sing their most complex compositions. Category: Urban Wildlife Photographer: Seth Forestson, UK Location: Lumphini Park, Bangkok, Thailand Forestson lowered himself onto the mud to capture this common water lizard against the city skyline. These adaptable lizards live in cities across South and South East Asia and will take whatever food is available, such as catfish and koi. Category: Under Water Photographer: Tony Wu, USA/Japan Location: Kagoshima Prefecture, Kyūshū, Japan This is probably the first time the courtship ritual of Abbott's moray eels has been photographed, the NHM said. Wu worked with biologists and used dim red light and a customised fisheye lens to minimise disturbance. Category: Photojournalist Story Award Photographer: Loren Elliott, USA Location: USA San Francisco is estimated to be home to around 100 coyotes, living alongside a large human population. While they can prey on domestic animals, they also help control disease-carrying rodents, and residents' attitudes towards them are mixed. Category: Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles Photographer: Anton Sorokin, US Location: Contra Costa County, California, USA Sorokin dipped his camera and lights in a murky pond to catch this glimpse of a California newt laying her eggs. Category : Behaviour: Invertebrates Photographer: Sitaram Raul, India Location: Thar Desert, Rajasthan, India A scorpion is photographed burrowing into the shifting dunes of India's Thar Desert. Exploring the dunes at night, Raul saw many scorpions searching for prey but as temperatures rose after sunrise, the scorpion dug into the sand to escape the intense heat. Category: Oceans: The Bigger Picture Photographer: Alex Lindbloom, USA Location: Off Cenderawasih Bay, Papua, Indonesia A whale shark investigates the catch of a mobile net-fishing platform, known as a bagan. Lindbloom searched for sharks around dawn, using the bagan's bright lights to illuminate them when there was too little natural light for his drone. Category: Plants and Fungi Photographer: Agorastos Papatsanis, Greece Location: Litochoro, Pieria, Greece Papatsanis used ultrviolet light to illuminate mushrooms known as "beautiful bonnets" growing from a decaying log on the lower slopes of Mount Olympus in Greece. Category: Rising Star Award Photographer: Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, Germany Location: Germany and Northern Ireland, UK Tinker-Tsavalas uses macro photography to reveal the intricate details of tiny animals that are easily overlooked, particularly in urban habitats. His interest in macro photography developed during the Covid-19 lockdowns, when he was restricted to habitats close to his home in Berlin. Category: Natural Artistry Photographer: Michał Michalski, Poland Location: Litochoro, Pieria, Greece Michalski used a slow shutter speed to photograph birds flying across a background of leafless birch trees. A field of unharvested sunflowers had attracted mixed flocks of birds, especially goldfinches and bramblings, before they were startled into the air by a sparrowhawk. Category: Wetlands: The Bigger Picture Photographer: Alex Visbal, Colombia Location: Stansbury Bay, Great Salt Lake, Utah, USA Visbal documents how a single engineered line can reshape an entire wetland as part of a long-term project on the industrial impact on waterways. The pink comes from microbes thriving in extremely salty water after the area was cut off from fresh water. Category: Photojournalism Photographer: Francisco Negroni, Chile Location: Route 40, Santa Cruz Province, Argentina Negroni records this scene of a dead puma displayed as a hunting trophy in Santa Cruz, a province in Argentine Patagonia. Although Santa Cruz banned puma hunting in 2025, illegal persecution continues. Category: Portfolio Award Photographer: Kutub Uddin, Bangladesh/UK Location: West Sussex, England, UK Uddin's photographs explore the miniature world of slime moulds, organisms that can be barely visible to the naked eye and whose fruiting structures are just one to two millimetres high. A four-year study of children's photographs over the generations and archive material go on display. This is the second year of the UKAHT's three-year mission to protect the historic base on Goudier Island in Antarctica. The winner of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year captures a rarely seen elephant behaviour, revealing the complexity of their emotional lives. The Charity Commission says it is aware of "financial concerns" relating to the rare-breeds charity. Hoo Zoo and Dinosaur World has been keeping news of the latest arrival secret until now. title: Turkish police raid opposition TV station, halting live broadcasts
content: Turkish police have raided the headquarters of one of the country's most-watched news channels, halting its live broadcasts. Reports in Turkish media said financial crimes police were searching the building of Halk TV, a pro-opposition channel, and that 11 people had been taken into custody in a raid linked to the channel's owner. The government also appointed a new administrator to run the channel. It is the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his government. Halk journalists were initially unable to get into the building, although they later were allowed in, several reporters said on X. There was a heavy police presence in the building, they said. Halk's news channel and live broadcasts on its YouTube page were both offline early on Wednesday. The channel has been seen by many in the country as being close to the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP). It often voices criticism of Erdoğan's ruling AK party. Prosecutors said arrest warrants had been issued for 17 people as part of the investigation into Halk chairman Cafer Mahiroğlu on allegations of bribery, rigging tenders and money laundering, Turkish media reported. Mahiroğlu, who was reportedly not in the country during the raid, wrote on social media that seven members of his family were among those detained. "Today is a dark day for Turkey," he said in a video message. "The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons." The Istanbul Bar Association denounced the move, which it noted came hours before Ekrem Imamoğlu, widely seen as Erdoğan's biggest political rival, was due to begin his defence against corruption charges in court, for which he has been in prison for over a year. Özgür Özel, leader of the opposition New Party, called the raid "weak and cowardly". "Storming a TV channel with a police raid at dawn and appointing a trustee is something only dictators do," he wrote on social media. Özel set up the party after being removed as the CHP's leader by a court in May and replaced by a party veteran who had previously been voted out, in a move which further cemented Erdoğan's grip on power. Turkey ranked 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) 2026 World Press Freedom Index . The organisation stated that 90% of national media outlets were under government control and criticised the "abusive prosecution" of critical publications in the country, which Erdoğan has led since 2003. The vast majority of Turkish media is seen as pro-government after years of state legal and financial pressure, corporate acquisitions and self-censorship. In September, a court ordered the blocking of access to the website and social media accounts of T24, on the grounds that it had published "LGBT propaganda". In October 2025, the authorities seized control of Tele1, another pro-opposition TV channel, appointing a trustee to oversee broadcasts, which were stripped of all hard-news content. The channel still exists but its pro-opposition stance has been completely neutralised. Four years after the attacks, Serhii Kuznetsov appears in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany. Elon Musk's system allows Kyiv to protect Ukrainian skies and effectively guide drones to Russian targets. With few details so far, it is unclear what might need to change for a Pope who has been focused on stability. Spain's exclave in North Africa is still dealing with the aftermath of an influx of 70,000 people from Morocco in July. Six crew members are rescued but 10 are missing after a merchant ship was sunk overnight, Bulgaria says. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Sydney teen charged with murder of boy who was shot in face
content: Australian police have charged a 19-year-old man with murder after a boy, aged 12, was fatally shot in the face and neck at a Sydney home last month. Police were called to a unit in Sydney's northwest on 21 September after reports of a shooting. The boy was rushed to hospital in a critical condition and died three days later. Nine people at the home when the shooting happened were uninjured. Three men - all aged 18 - were arrested and two later released without charge. The third man, Isaac Bechara, who has since turned 19, was initially charged with concealing a serious indictable offence and remanded in custody. On Tuesday, police charged him with murder. Bechara did not apply for bail when he appeared in court on Wednesday. In the immediate aftermath of the shooting, New South Wales (NSW) police ruled out links to organised crime but days later, investigators said they were looking at possible gangland connections. "A number of individuals that were inside the unit at the time are well known to NSW Police and their association with organised crime is being considered by investigators," said Supt Naomi Moore last month. Moore added that some of the people who were present at the time of the shooting were "not currently co-operating with investigators" and that police were yet to recover the firearm. Local media reported that the incident was a suspected accident, citing police sources, and that the boy's father had paid tribute to his son on social media, posting a photo of the pair with the caption, "RIP my baby". When the boy's death was announced, NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said any incident "where we lose a young life in those circumstances is tragic". Goodman Group, the property giant behind the Project Mars data centre, says the decision is due to changes to the "policy and regulatory environment". A man's confession to abducting UK toddler Cheryl Grimmer in Australia was previously thrown out. Wednesday's fatal shooting of a man in his 40s comes after a university student was gunned down on Tuesday. Cheryl Grimmer's family have been petitioning police to consider the new evidence they say they've found. Julian Ingram is wanted over the shooting deaths of three people, including his pregnant former partner. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
content: Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged. The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club. Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal. The PM, who was mayor until June, sparked widespread controversy when he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up. On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade. The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany. It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions". But the statement did not specify that this referred to two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches. A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at £300 for hospitality. Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately £699. Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a £150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018. But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term. BBC News has asked GMCA for more details about this policy - given its website has entries dating back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024. Downing Street has defended the two dinners with Man City's chairman, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman. But political pressure on Burnham to be clearer about any former discussions with Man City is continuing to mount. Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City. "This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football." And Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners". Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded for several days that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club. Burnham told the Rest Is Politics podcast last week he was "happy" to do this and would "quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester". "None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021." Asked at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday whether anyone at the club had raised the charges they were facing with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me." With the PM continuing to face pressure on the issue, he told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full", referring to the GMCA's statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club". When asked by reporters why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings", the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement. The list of meetings, which was published by the GMCA on Monday, did not include detail on what was discussed. The BBC has asked GMCA why the two dinners were not specifically mentioned. In September Man City - which has dominated the top flight of English football for years - was found guilty by an independent commission of breaching Premier League financial regulations. The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations. Sanctions are yet to be announced and City, which denies any wrongdoing, has lodged an appeal against the verdict. Earlier this month, Sir Richard Leese - who was head of Manchester City Council for 25 years until 2021 - defended a decade-old deal between the council and Man City owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG). Under the partnership between the authority and the company, which is linked to the United Arab Emirates royal family, land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates", according to a University of Sheffield report. Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond. Bev Craig says the city region needs to plan for the future and this means going underground. Bev Craig says people from across all 10 boroughs had complained to her about potholes. Bev Craig says planning rules should be reviewed after complaints about warehouses built near housing. The mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, has issued a "call to action" to public bodies. Mayor Bev Craig said interested parties can apply for a share of the £20m pot later this year. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. title: UK resists EU pressure to hit China with tariffs
content: The business secretary has hit back at European demands for British tariffs on Chinese imports, saying the government will not change its trade rules because of pressure from Brussels. Jonathan Reynolds warned that the government would not bow to calls from other countries for the UK to hit Chinese vehicles with import taxes, despite political pressure to align with the EU in exchange for deeper future economic ties. The EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024 and last Friday agreed a 350,000 a year quota on Chinese hybrid cars amid fears cheaper alternatives are causing deindustrialisation and job losses. Reynolds conceded that levying sanctions on Chinese goods was an option in the future, but he dismissed concerns from Brussels that the UK could provide a back door to the European market. His comments highlight the divisions that remain between the UK and EU on trade and industrial policy, which could derail the prime minister’s attempts to move closer to Brussels. “I just want to be clear: when we make any trade decision in terms of trade defence tariffs in relation to the EU, that’s based on the UK interest – it’s not based on any other country asking for that,” said Reynolds during a trade trip to India. “In 2024, [we] looked at this issue carefully, and we keep it under review depending on what the needs of industry are … But it comes down to what is the fundamental nature of the UK automotive sector. It’s an export-led sector, so that’s what I’ve got to take into account.” With Europe having imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese electric cars, some believe that the UK has opened an alternative route into the EU for Chinese companies setting up in the UK to sell into the bloc. Nissan, for instance, has agreed to look at building cars in northern England for the Chinese manufacturer Chery . Reynolds rebutted those accusations, however, saying: “The UK currently has no major Chinese manufacturer based in its automotive sector, so we’re not making vehicles here and sending them to the single market through some sort of back door.” His comments raise the stakes ahead of intense final weeks of negotiations before the long-awaited UK-EU summit, which Andy Burnham confirmed this week would be held in Brussels on 20 November. The prime minister told the Commons on Monday he wanted a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s place in Europe, as he framed the summit as a possible first step to EU membership. The new Made in Europe trade rules aim to protect European companies from subsidised Chinese imports, but British manufacturers worry they will also be shut out of supply chains. The issue will not formally be on the agenda at the November summit, but British officials are hoping to use those talks to shape the European legislation. Diplomats on both sides of the Channel say the summit will now be an early test of whether Burnham’s desire for a “real reset” in UK-EU relations is likely to bear fruit. One EU official said this week that the UK’s negotiating position would determine whether it was worth pursuing more fundamental changes such as British access to the single market, a new customs union or re-accession. Some in Brussels have been pushing for Britain to levy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in return for getting access to the European market under the new trade rules. Reynolds has previously dismissed such an option in part because of the risk that Beijing could hit the UK with reciprocal tariffs, damaging British companies such as Jaguar Land Rover. He said it would be to Europe’s detriment if it did not admit the UK into the scheme. “If you look at the impact analysis of such a policy, the consequences for the EU [of] excluding the UK are much more difficult,” he said. “This is not just in the UK’s interest; it’s not in the EU’s interest because obviously we have integrated supply chains.” Reynolds said the summit was an important milestone in EU-UK relations but also insisted that new trading terms for electricity, emissions and food and drink products would be a major achievement in themselves. Speaking from a two-day trade delegation to Delhi and Mumbai, he acknowledged that the landmark free trade agreement he helped strike last year with India would become defunct if Britain does rejoin the EU. “Obviously, if you enter those arrangements, you are doing things collectively. So there would be trade relationships with the UK that were based on Europe, the EU as a whole – that is how the European Union works in terms of its relationship. “That’s why obviously when we were part of it, we didn’t have these separate bespoke arrangements.” But he insisted that it remained worth continuing to push to broaden the scope of the agreement, as he unveiled a series of UK-India investments which officials say are worth over £1bn to the UK over the next 15 years. The deal has already begun to reduce the price of Scotch whisky in Indian shops, after tariffs were reduced from 150% to 75%. Now British officials are keen to free up trade in services as well as goods, for example, pushing for both countries to recognise each other’s legal qualifications. “There are some specific things regarding who can practice law and in which area,” Reynolds said. “I am confident over the medium to long term that this will improve over time.” He added: “We’ve got to be cognisant of this long-term position with the EU.
